articles.title: ‘We’re not going to back down’: tiny Dorset B&B stands up to Airbnb’s legal bid to ‘monopolise’ letters ‘bnb’
articles.summary: Three little letters - bnb-side’s name is a play on the local b-side arts festival, but Silicon Valley colossus sees threat to global brand. In one corner is bnb-side, a six-room bed and breakfast on the Isle of Portland – a tiny wedge of limestone tied by a narrow ribbon of shingle to the Dorset…
body: On the other is Airbnb, the San Francisco-based booking colossus. The battle between them is over the three little letters they share.

b-side says the “bnb” in bnb-side means what it has always meant: bed and breakfast. But lawyers for the Silicon Valley titan say the name of the guesthouse, perched on an outcrop just 4 miles long by 1.5 miles wide, threatens the global brand of the $100bn heavyweight.

“We thought the name was both really obvious and really cool,” said Rocca Holly-Nambi, director of b-side. “b-side was founded almost 20 years ago, so when we set up our BnB in 2024 to raise money for the festival, we just popped the ‘bn’ in front because it’s a universally recognised description of what we’re offering.”

Airbnb doesn’t agree. In May, it sent the first of three legal letters to the tiny social enterprise to demand it cease its attempt to register the B&B using the name it had used since it opened its doors.

articles.title: Goody Goody review – intriguing natural childbirth horror lurches into demonic occult blowout
articles.summary: After Samantha Robinson decides a forest cabin in deep winter is the perfect spot to bear her child, it’s going to be a very bad shift for the doula and midwife. Conception, pregnancy and childbirth are defining human experiences, and so remain perennial themes for horror, from Rosemary’s Baby to…
body: Goody (Samantha Robinson) is in the pool, ready for battle, soaking in good vibes beamed at her by husband Jayson (Colby Hollman), his doula sister Candace (Zoe Renee) and their rock, midwife Sarah (Colleen Foy). But shaken by weirdly spaced contractions, Sarah takes Jason aside and admits that she has a bad feeling. It’s not purely premonition: a flashback reveals, in contrast to the new-age love-in around the tub, Goody’s insistence against Sarah’s advice that she give birth in winter at their forest cabin. The midwife fears it will make going to hospital too difficult should anything go wrong – and only agrees to supervise because Goody will probably go ahead solo if she pulls out.

Creamer starts out by layering telling details that insinuate the stifling boho perfectionism ruling this household: a faux Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan cover featuring the couple, their disdain for teabags, the cloying veneer of positivity. He films the damning flashback with psychological finesse to show Jayson’s status as junior partner; back on the natal frontline, Candace sometimes slips into a grandstanding bolshiness that threatens to tip Sarah’s carefully nurtured equilibrium out of balance.

articles.title: Burrata and beyond: a foodie tour of northern Puglia, Italy
articles.summary: It’s the birthplace of the popular cheese, but the Barletta-Andria-Trani province in southern Italy has an array of local delicacies – from olive oil and yellow tomatoes to goat prosciutto. ‘I don’t eat mozzarella outside Puglia,” says our friend Savio.
body: Puglia is also the birthplace of ingredient du jour burrata, which originated in Andria, a few miles from Savio’s home town of Barletta. Andria forms one part of the triangular Barletta-Andria-Trani (BAT) province, often passed over for better-known parts of Puglia, despite the cheese connection and Barletta having miles of palm-backed, sandy beaches.

About a century ago, in the hills outside Andria, farmer Lorenzo Bianchino was snowed in and couldn’t get his milk to market. To save what he could, he revived an old technique for preserving butter ( burro, hence burrata), stuffing cream mixed with mozzarella scraps ( stracciatella ) in a casing of the stretched-curd cheese.

articles.title: Is it true that … having a hot drink will cool you down?
articles.summary: A warm cup of tea can trigger sweating and lower your body temperature, but only if you’re in an airy space. Could a warm cup of tea really be the key to cooling down in hot weather?
body: Prof John Tregoning, the author of Live Forever? A Curious Scientist’s Guide to Wellness, Ageing and Death, says it depends on the circumstances. He points to the work of Australian scientist Prof Ollie Jay, who is a world leader in researching heat and how it balances out in your body.
When it comes to drinking a hot beverage, there are two effects on your body. “You’ve got the heat that the drink gives you, and then the amount that you sweat as a result of it,” Tregoning says.
While you’re consuming the warm drink, its high temperature will cause your body temperature to rise. That elevated temperature will trigger you to sweat more.
This is where things become complicated. Sweat cools down the body when it evaporates. When water on the skin turns to gas, it takes heat energy away from the body.

articles.title: How Jane Wade Used Google AI For Her New York Fashion Week Show
articles.summary: After partnering with A24 on creative workflows for film, Google is setting its sights on fashion. New York designers Jane Wade and Sergio Hudson were first to co-develop tools to cut costs and time in the run up to their SS27 shows.
body: After partnering with A24 to co-develop workflows for the film sector, Google’s Envisioning Studio set its sights on the fashion sector. Ahead of New York Fashion Week, Google partnered with designers Jane Wade and Sergio Hudson to develop and test two fashion-specific tools for pre-show styling and runway visualization in beta mode through its Flow AI creative studio.

“Our core premise is that technology must be built with creatives, not simply thrown over the wall at them,” says Yeawon Choi, the user experience designer within Google’s Envisioning Studio who led the project. “We co-design with the creative that will use these tools because we want them to be helpful. And across creative industries, from fashion to film, we’ve found similar friction points — all centering on pre-visualization, relentless timelines, and steep resource constraints.”

articles.title: How Carolina Herrera Pulled Off a Succession Success Story
articles.summary: Carolina Herrera, which turns 45 this year, is a blueprint for how to gracefully transition from its founder to a new creative director: Wes Gordon. Gordon and president Emilie Rubinfeld share how they did it.
body: Wes Gordon’s eight-year run at Carolina Herrera is often looked at as one of the most successful succession stories in fashion, an industry rife with designer turnover where founder exits can get ugly. Speaking over Zoom ahead of the house’s Spring/Summer 2027 runway show at New York Fashion Week on Monday, Gordon often returns to a word that helps to explain why: respect.
“The crucial ingredient for a transition is respect,” Gordon continues. “And I think when you see examples of transitions that go awry, maybe there was respect missing from the equation.”

articles.title: Could Sabyasachi Be India’s First Global Luxury House?
articles.summary: Sabyasachi Mukherjee makes his return to New York Fashion Week on Tuesday, 20 years after his last outing in the city. But this time, he is competing as a more mature luxury player.
body: The brand made its runway debut at Lakmé Fashion Week in Mumbai in 2002, with a collection called Kashgar Bazaar, focusing on Indian textile traditions in the form of Western shapes and Indian ensembles. It soon made the move into the big leagues, first in Milan and then in New York in 2006, where Mukherjee brought an artisanal collection called Snail, built around the idea of “slow fashion”, to the States.

That first New York outing came with a lesson: a label must be absolute at home before it can be truly international. It’s a high-stakes test for Indian fashion. No Indian designer has yet built a house with the scale, retail footprint, or cultural authority to compete as a genuine global luxury player.
Now, as he gears up to show in Tribeca this week, Mukherjee is betting he can be the first.

articles.title: KidSuper’s Colm Dillane Took Over Brooklyn City Hall to Celebrate the Borough’s Fashion Talent—With a Surprise Performance from Lauryn Hill
articles.summary: Brooklyn borough president Antonio Reynoso and designer Colm Dillane shone a spotlight on local talent at a fashion show that featured a performance by Lauryn Hill.
body: Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso was hyping up the crowd on Saturday night for The People’s Runway, a community-focused fashion show that highlights talent from the city’s sprawling district (and, to many, its creative hub). “This isn’t golf, this isn’t tennis; if you like something, make some noise!”
“As someone who's gone through the fashion industry and seen what helps and what hurts, I’m trying to create something that I knew could benefit designers.”

The fullest expression of Dillane’s role is The People’s Runway, held on the steps of the Borough Hall—a Greek Revival building at the edge of Brooklyn Heights and Downtown Brooklyn—which takes five designers (from a pool of over 300 applicants) and, most visibly, gives them a platform to display their work. Additionally, it awards each with $15,000 in funds, plus the potential of more with partnership deals, and mentorship. Launched last year, it was supposed to be a one-off event, but proved so successful that it’s now planned to be an annual occurrence.
